subject: Post-call: first-payload latency probe & fallback plan (BrightPath)
messages:
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>

Cc: BrightPath SRE <ops@brightpath.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>

Subject: Post-call: first-payload latency probe & fallback plan (BrightPath)

Thanks again for the sync today — good coverage on the app flow and where TTFT matters most. Notes and proposed next steps below. Please confirm anything I mis-summarized.

Quick recap of our performance ask from the call:
- Primary goal: minimize time-to-first-payload (TTFP) for streaming responses (not just final token). BrightPath target = median <= 120 ms on cold-ish traffic, 95th <= 250 ms.
- Preferred transport: WebSocket (low head-of-line risk) with SSE as an acceptable fallback if browser/edge constraints require it.
- Chunk cadence: small initial chunk within the TTFP budget (single partial payload ~100-200 bytes) followed by 200–400 ms pacing for subsequent chunks for interactive UIs.
- Concurrency target: 400–600 concurrent active streams per region during peak; sustained throughput ~120 qps with short bursts to 1k.
- Quality constraints: cannot quantize below FP16-equivalent for the final scoring model; can evaluate int8 for prefilter/embedding models.

Proposed Redwood plan / test approach:
1) We’ll run a focused latency probe from our hosted test harness to your staging endpoint: 1k synthetic sessions over 15 minutes across us-west/us-east to reproduce concurrency profile.
2) Measure TTFP (first payload arrival) by transport (WS vs SSE) and by cache state (cold vs warm KV cache). We’ll report median / 95th / p99.
3) Validate chunk cadence under sustained streams and confirm per-connection token pacing.
4) If WS meets TTFP but has occasional spikes, we’ll test an automatic-transport-fallback policy (WS primary, SSE fallback) for sticky sessions.

Action items — please: 
- Send a representative set of sample payloads (prompt sizes, typical context lengths, and any system-level prefills).
- Share a staging API key or test endpoint and an ops contact so we can run the probe (ops@brightpath.ai).
- Confirm whether BrightPath wants Dedicated reserved capacity for the pilot or to validate on hosted.

I attached the streaming-test-plan (xlsx) with the proposed scenarios. If you’re aligned, we’ll schedule the probe for Friday and share a short runbook + expected metrics.

Thanks,
Stephanie Nguyen
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-call: first-payload latency probe & fallback plan (BrightPath)

Thanks Stephanie — that matches our conversation. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Our internal SLO is to keep user-visible first payload <= 120 ms median, but we can tolerate up to 300 ms p95 for long-context requests.
- We strongly prefer WebSocket for the desktop client and will use SSE for older mobile webviews where WS is flaky. Fallback logic is OK as long as session affinity is preserved.
- Concurrency: target 500 steady-state active streams across two regions (us-west/us-east) with ability to burst to 1k for flash loads.
- Cold start behavior: our front-end commonly spins up a new worker per session; we’d like Redwood to test both fully cold and warmed-KV scenarios.

We can provide the sample prompts (will upload to ops@brightpath.ai) and will generate a test API key restricted to your probe IPs. Ops will also share our staging endpoint and a small set of real traces for you to model pacing.

If possible, start with a hosted run so we can validate the behavior before committing to Dedicated. We’ll revisit Dedicated if warm-cache economics show significant gains.

—Elena
Elena Moreno
Head of Product, BrightPath AI
elena@brightpath.ai

Subject: FWD: Post-call: first-payload latency probe & fallback plan (BrightPath)

Looping in Marcus for engineering feasibility and quick ops plan. High-level thoughts: 

- Probe design: we should run two passes — cold start (no KV cache warmed, fresh process) and warm (pre-warmed KV + steady-state batching). For fairness, record CPU/GPU utilization and kernel selection logs.
- Transport: WebSocket will typically win TL; however, JS runtime/network stacks on some mobile devices add jitter; we should instrument per-transport jitter and add a head-of-line mitigation (smaller first chunk).
- Chunk cadence: propose sending an initial partial delta within 80–100 ms (if model produces something) then structured micro-chunks every 150–300 ms for the next 2s. If downstream rendering wants heavier smoothing, we can offer a 300–400 ms cadence mode.
- Concurrency: recommend starting the test at 400 concurrent connections and ramp to 800; observe tail latency and request queuing behavior.

I attached a quick SLO matrix that maps observed TTFP to recommended config (dedicated pool size, batch windows, KV warmers). Marcus — can you validate whether our hosted test harness can emulate ixp-regional latency egress to their staging endpoints? Also, please confirm whether we can instrument first-payload timings in the kernel (should be okay but need minor agent changes).

If all good, I’ll schedule the probe Fri 07/23 in the morning and sync with ops@brightpath.ai for API key / IP allowlist.

Thanks — Ben
Ben Carter
